title: Chapter 54: The Night of Masks, Part 2 of 5: Under the Dome
html:
The first thing was the warmth. The second thing was the smell. The third thing was the light, and after that Lyra stopped being able to count.
They went up the plum-colored carpet on the steps, between the torches, with the Duke's great soft arm under her gloved hand and his rings cold through the gray kid. Past the six Watch constables, who did not look at them. Past the porters in plum, who bowed. Through the bronze doors, which were taller than the house on Crown Walk and carved all over with shapes she did not have time to see. And into the warmth.
It came at her like a wall. After the cold of the street, after the snow and the torches and the wind off the river, it was like walking into a bath. Hot, heavy, still air, full of the breath of five hundred people and the heat of a thousand candles and the great iron stoves she could not see but could feel, somewhere under the floor, pushing the heat up through gratings. Her face under the mask began to burn at once. She felt the quiet hold it still.
And the smell. Wax, first. Beeswax, from the candles. Then scent. Every scent there was. Lilies and roses and violets and musk and orange-flower water and something heavy and sweet and smoky that she did not know, all of them at once, coming off five hundred bodies in silk and velvet, so thick in the hot air that she could taste it. Then wine. Then hot sugar, from somewhere, burning a little. And under all of it, very faint, so faint that she would not have known it if she had not smelled it every day for a week in the crypt of Saint Bride's, something sweet and soft. Like pears going over in a dish.
She stopped walking. The Duke stopped with her. He did not say anything. He just stood, and waited, and let her breathe.
Then she looked up.
The hall of the Memory Bourse was round.
She had known that. Corin had told her. Gideon had drawn it on the crypt floor in blue chalk. She had not known what it would be like to stand in it. It was enormous. A great round room, so wide that the far side of it was lost in the haze of candle smoke and heat, with a floor of black and white marble squares, like the floor of the hall on Crown Walk, but a hundred times bigger, going away from her in every direction like a chessboard for giants. And above it, the dome.
From inside, it was not a bubble. It was a sky. A great curved sky of glass, a hundred feet up, held up by thin black iron ribs that went up from the edges of the room and met at the top in a ring, like the spokes of an umbrella, or the lines on the inside of a shell. And between the ribs, a thousand panes of glass. And beyond the glass, the night. Black. With the snow coming down on it, very slowly, and the light from the hall going up through the glass and catching the flakes as they fell, so that they looked like sparks. Like ash. Like a sky full of falling gold.
And hanging down from the very top of the dome, from the iron ring where the ribs met, on a chain so long and thin she could hardly see it, a chandelier. The biggest she had ever seen. A great cloud of glass drops and silver arms and candles, a hundred candles, more, all burning, turning very slowly on its chain in the hot air rising from the floor, so that the light swung and slid and glittered over everything below.
Round the edge of the room, all the way round, high up, under the curve of the dome, there was a gallery. A narrow balcony with a gilded rail, and behind the rail, curtains. Plum-colored velvet. Drawn back, here and there, so that she could see into little boxes behind them, like the boxes at the theatre. People sat in some of them. Masked. Looking down.
And in the very middle of the room, under the very middle of the dome, under the chandelier, standing by itself on the black and white floor in a little clear space with nobody near it, there was a box.
Brass. As big as a coffin standing on its end. Square and plain and polished so bright that it shone like gold. It had a slot in the top, a long narrow slot like the slot in a poor box in a church, and nothing else. No handle. No lock. No hinge that she could see.
The brass bid box.
And round it, on the floor, in a circle, a ring of black squares. A wider ring than the rest. As if the chessboard had a hole in the middle, and somebody had put a lid on it.
The third door is not a door. It is the floor.
She made herself look away.
Round the room, between the bronze doors and the brass box, in a great ring, there were tables. Long tables of glass on gilded legs, with plum-colored velvet laid down the middle of each one. And on the velvet, in rows, with little white cards in front of them, the lots.
They were vials.
Hundreds of them. Small glass vials, each no bigger than her finger, stoppered with wax, standing on the velvet in rows like soldiers. And each one glowed.
That was what the light was. Not just the candles. The vials. Each one had something in it, a soft moving light, like smoke, like mist, like a tiny cloud with the sun inside it. And each one was a different color. Some gold. Some blue. Some a pale soft green like new leaves. Some rose. Some white. Some a deep dark red, like wine held up to a fire. They glowed on the plum velvet all round the room, hundreds of them, and the light of them came up into the faces of the people bending over them, so that every masked face in the room was lit from below, softly, in a different color.
Lyra went to the nearest table. She did not decide to. Her feet took her.
The Duke came with her. He did not say anything. He just stood beside her, huge and silent and smelling of lavender, and let her look.
The cards were written in a beautiful clerk's hand, black ink on white, the same hand as the Lady's list.
Lot 1. A Childhood. Rural. A farm in the east, summers by a river, a brown dog, a grandmother's kitchen, the smell of bread. Aged four to nine. Whole. Clean. Reserve: three hundred crowns.
The vial in front of it was gold. Soft, warm, slowly turning gold, like late sun through a window.
Lot 2. A Childhood. Harbor. Ships, gulls, a father who came home in the spring. Aged five to eight. Lightly worn. Reserve: two hundred crowns.
Blue-gray. Moving like water.
Lot 9. A Talent. The violin. Twenty years' practice. Concert standard. Whole. To be placed only by a licensed hand. Reserve: one thousand crowns.
Deep red.
Lot 12. Courage, common. A lot of six. Small fears overcome: dogs, heights, the dark, speaking in company. Suitable for a nervous child. Reserve: sixty crowns the lot.
Six little vials, side by side, each a pale clear silver.
Lot 17. A Love. First. Aged sixteen. A boy at a fair. Three summers. Ended kindly. Reserve: four hundred crowns.
Rose. The softest, palest rose. It moved in its glass like breath.
Lyra stood in front of Lot 17 for a long time.
She thought of a boy at a fair. Of three summers. Of somebody, somewhere in the city, who had loved somebody at sixteen and been loved back, and had had it ended kindly, and had kept it, all their life, the way you keep a pressed flower in a book. And then one day had needed three hundred crowns more than they needed it. Or had not been asked.
And a lady from the Hill would buy it tonight, in a mask, for four hundred crowns, and take it home in her reticule, and have it placed by a licensed hand, and remember, for the rest of her life, a boy at a fair she had never met.
She felt the quiet hold her face very still.
"Wine, your Grace?"
The voice was at her elbow. Low and dry and a little sour. A voice she knew. She did not turn her head.
A tall man in gold livery was standing beside the Duke with a tray in his white-gloved hands. On the tray, a decanter of cut glass, very old, full of something pale gold, and two glasses. He held the tray very steady. He stood with his weight on his right leg and his left leg out stiff a little to one side. His face was long and narrow and sour, with a short pointed gray beard.
"Fenton," said the Duke, without looking at him. "Thank you. The Marrowmere, I hope?"
"The Marrowmere, your Grace. The forty-one."
"Splendid."
The tall man poured. He poured beautifully, the way a man pours who has been pouring wine for thirty-one years, without spilling a drop, the decanter tilting and the pale gold wine going into the glass in a thin bright rope and stopping exactly at the right place. He gave a glass to the Duke. And then he turned, with the tray, and held out the second glass to her.
Lyra took it.
And as she took it, her gloved fingers, in Madame Hesper's thin gray kid, touched his. White cotton. Under the stem of the glass. Just for a moment. As if by accident.
She felt his finger move. Against hers. Once. And then twice, quick.
Then he had taken his hand away, and bowed, very slightly, the stiff sour bow of a servant who has done this a thousand times and does not much care for any of it. And turned, and limped away into the crowd with his tray, swinging his stiff left leg from the hip. And the crowd took him. And she could not see him any more. Just a gold coat among a hundred other coats, plum and blue and green and gold, going away between the glass tables under the falling-gold sky of the dome.
She looked down at the wine in her glass.
Pale gold. Like the light in Lot 1. Like late sun through a window.
She did not drink it.
"Marrowmere," said the Duke softly beside her. "From my mother's cellar. The year I came home." He looked at his own glass. "I bring it every year. I pour one glass, and I hold it all night, and I don't drink it either." He was quiet for a moment. "It reminds me that I came home. That's all. Some years that's quite a lot."
And above them, in the gallery, a curtain moved.
The Lady in Violet
The curtain that had moved was the biggest one in the gallery, on the far side of the dome, opposite the bronze doors. It was drawn back now, all the way, on both sides, and held back with thick gold cords. And behind it there was a box. Not like the others. Wider. Deeper. With a chair in it.
And a woman standing up out of the chair.
The room did not go quiet. Not then. But it changed. Lyra felt it change, the way you feel the air change before a storm. Five hundred people in masks, talking and laughing and bending over the glowing vials, and every one of them, without stopping, without turning round, became a little more careful. Voices went down. Laughter got shorter. Heads did not turn, but eyes did, behind the masks, up, to the gallery. To the big box opposite the doors. To the woman standing up out of the chair.
Lady Vivienne came to the gilded rail and put her hands on it and looked down.
She was not young. That was the first thing Lyra thought. She had expected, somehow, that she would be young. She was not. She was a woman of fifty, perhaps more, tall and very straight, with a long pale face and a long pale neck. Her hair was dark, nearly black, and it was dressed high on her head, very high, in a great smooth shining shape like a dome, like the dome above her, held up with pins of jet. Her gown was violet. Not plum, like her servants. Violet. Deep and rich and shining, the color of the sky over the river just after the sun has gone, and cut low at the neck, and close at the waist, and falling in heavy folds to the floor of the box.
And round her throat, lights.
A necklace. Not of stones. Of vials. Tiny ones, smaller than the ones on the tables, no bigger than a barleycorn, a dozen of them, hung on a fine black chain, close round her long pale neck. And every one glowed. Gold and blue and green and rose and white and red. They sat against her skin like little lamps, and threw small colored lights up into her face from below, so that her chin was green and her cheek was gold and the hollow of her throat was rose.
She did not wear a mask.
She had a fan. Black lace, on sticks of black wood. She held it closed, in one hand, on the rail.
And behind her, at her shoulder, a little back, in the shadow of the curtain, a young man stood. Thin and pale and very still, in a plain gray coat, with gray gloves on his hands. Dark eyes. Close-cropped hair. A small dark stain on the cuff of his right sleeve, which Lyra could not see from here but knew was there. Ink.
Remy.
He was not looking at the room. He was looking at the back of Lady Vivienne's head. At the great dark dome of her hair. His face was quite empty.
Lady Vivienne opened her fan.
It made no sound. But the room went quiet then. All of it. All at once. As if somebody had opened a door onto the snow and let the silence in. Five hundred masks turned up toward the gallery. The quartet that had been playing somewhere, very softly, behind a screen of palms in pots, stopped in the middle of a bar.
"My friends," said Lady Vivienne.
Her voice was low and dry and carried to every corner of the great round room without her seeming to raise it. A cool voice. Pleasant. The voice of a woman who has never in her life had to say anything twice.
"Welcome to the Bourse. Welcome to Midwinter. Another year." She looked down at them. At all of them. Slowly, round the room, from left to right, as if she were counting. "Another year, and here we all are. Still. In spite of everything. In spite of the Watch, and the Council, and the Health, and the weather, and the price of coal." A little ripple of laughter went round the room. She did not smile. "In spite of the Ministry, which is here tonight in such strength, to keep us all safe."
The laughter went quiet.
She turned her head a little, along the gallery, to the right. To a box three along from her own, with its curtain half drawn. And Lyra, following her eyes, saw who was in it.
Two figures. Side by side, at the rail. Both masked in white. Plain white, smooth, with no ornament at all. One in gray. A slight man of middle height, with thin fair hair going gray, and a plain gray coat, sitting very relaxed in a gilt chair with one arm along the rail. And one in white. All in white. A long white coat with a high collar and a row of silver buttons down the front, twelve of them, catching the light of the chandelier. A young woman, very straight, with fair hair pinned up tight under the ribbons of her white mask, and her hands folded on the rail in white kid gloves.
The man in gray lifted one hand from the rail, a little, toward Lady Vivienne. Like a man acknowledging a friend across a street.
And put it down again. Flat on the rail. And Lyra saw the finger move.
She did not need to see it twice.
Lady Vivienne looked at him for a moment. Her long pale face did not change. Then she turned back to the room.
"The lots are on the tables," she said. "You may look until the eleventh bell. At the eleventh bell, the bidding. Your cards, into the box. Sealed. As always." She closed her fan. "At a quarter before midnight, the Fourth Tier. And at midnight—" She paused. "At midnight I shall open the box, and read you the names. And you will all applaud. And then we shall dance until we cannot stand. As always."
She looked round the room once more. Slowly. From left to right.
And for a moment, just for a moment, as her eyes went round, they stopped.
Not on Lyra. Lyra saw that, with a great cold rush of relief. Not on the Duke. On something behind them. Past them. On the far side of the room, to the left of the bronze doors, under the gallery, where the wall was hung with plum velvet from the gallery rail to the floor. Lyra could not see anything there. Just velvet. Plum, in long heavy folds. And a pair of men in plum livery, porters, standing in front of it with their hands behind their backs, very still. Two of them. One on each side of a place where the velvet was a little darker, a little heavier, in a tall narrow shape, like the shape of a door.
Lady Vivienne's eyes stopped there. And something happened in her long pale face. Lyra could not have said what. It did not move. Nothing moved. But for one breath, perhaps two, it looked like the face of a woman who has been told, an hour ago, something she did not want to know, and has had an hour to make her face not show it, and has almost managed.
Then the eyes went on round. And came back to the room.
"Enjoy yourselves, my friends," said Lady Vivienne. "It is Midwinter."
And she opened her fan again, and the quartet behind the palms began again in the middle of the bar where it had stopped, and the room breathed out, and the voices came back, and the laughter, louder than before. And Lady Vivienne turned round in her box, and sat down in her chair, and Remy bent down to her ear and said something. And she did not answer him.
"Well," said the Duke softly, beside Lyra. "Well, well."
She looked at him.
He was looking where Lady Vivienne had looked. At the plum velvet on the far wall, to the left of the doors. At the two porters. At the tall narrow darker place between them, like the shape of a door.
"Forty years I've come to this house," said the Duke. "Forty Midwinters. I've never once seen her look at that wall." He lifted his glass of Marrowmere and did not drink it. "There's a garden behind it, you know. A little one. Very old. Between the Bourse and the river wall. Nobody uses it. There's a door from it into the hall, behind that velvet, that's been shut since before I was born."
Lyra did not say anything.
Ninth bell. The Bourse. Masked. By the garden door, not the front. The Lady to be told at the eighth bell, and not before.
Across the river, very far away, through the glass of the dome and the falling snow, the great bell of the Ministry began to ring the ninth hour.
And the two porters in front of the plum velvet, on the far wall, to the left of the bronze doors, took one step apart.
